title: Cut Into Three, Pay Each Opener
statement:
You get an array nums. Cut it into exactly 3 non-empty contiguous pieces, keeping the original order. Each piece costs its first element.

Return the smallest possible total cost of the three pieces.

examples.why: Pieces [5], [4], [3, 9] cost 5 + 4 + 3. The first piece always starts with the 5.
Pieces [2, 9], [8], [1] cost 2 + 8 + 1. Taking the first three elements as openers would cost 19.
Both 1s can open a piece: [7], [1], [1, 8]. Equal values are fine.

hints: The first piece must start at index 0, so nums[0] is always paid. What decides the other two costs?
Choosing where pieces 2 and 3 start is the same as choosing two different indices i < j after 0. Any such pair works.
So the answer is nums[0] plus the two smallest values among nums[1..]. One pass with two running minimums finds them.

explain.intuition:
The cost only depends on where each piece starts. Piece one always starts at index 0. Pieces two and three start at some indices i < j, both at least 1, and every such pair gives a valid cut. There is no other constraint, so you just want the two cheapest start positions after index 0.

That makes the answer nums[0] + smallest + second smallest of the rest. Positions do not matter, and two equal values at different indices can both be used. You can sort the tail, but tracking the two smallest values in one pass is O(n) and O(1) space.
steps: For each value v in nums[1..]: if v < first, shift first into second and set first = v; else if v < second, set second = v.
pitfalls: Including nums[0] among the candidates for the two smallest. It is already paid as the first opener.
Using v <= first carelessly or skipping duplicates. In [7, 1, 1, 8] both 1s count.
Thinking the pieces must have similar lengths. Only the openers matter.

solutions.title: Try every pair of cut points
solutions.idea: Pick the start i of piece two and the start j of piece three. Pay nums[0] + nums[i] + nums[j] and keep the minimum.

solutions.title: Two smallest after the first
solutions.idea: Openers two and three can be any two later positions, so take the two smallest values of nums[1..].

followups: Cut into k pieces instead of 3. Does the same idea still work?
Now the last two openers must be at most d positions apart. What structure keeps the smallest values inside a sliding window?
